Cartilage-hair hypoplasia

Mendelian MONDO:0009595 Pathograph 70 Show in embeddings browser osteochondrodysplasia immuno-osseous dysplasia autosomal recessive disease

Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is an autosomal recessive immuno-osseous dysplasia caused by biallelic variants in the noncoding RNA gene RMRP. Its variable manifestations include metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, disproportionate short stature, fine or sparse hair, immune dysfunction, anemia, Hirschsprung disease and increased malignancy risk. Promoter variants can reduce RNA expression, while transcribed-region variants can impair RNase MRP complex function. Studies demonstrate defective pre-rRNA processing, altered ribosome abundance and cell-proliferation defects; the contributions of mRNA turnover, small-RNA regulation and telomere homeostasis to individual tissues remain incompletely resolved. Immune dysfunction may become clinically apparent in adulthood, and malignancy can occur without preceding clinical immune symptoms.

Inheritance

1
Autosomal recessive inheritance HP:0000007
CHH is autosomal recessive, arising from biallelic variants in RMRP. Heterozygous carriers are asymptomatic and do not show the cellular proliferation defect, although telomerase activity is reduced in carriers in a gene-dose-dependent manner, so the carrier state is not entirely silent at every molecular level. Each sib of an affected individual has a 25% recurrence risk.
Autosomal recessive inheritance

"Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is an autosomal recessive syndromic immunodeficiency with skeletal dysplasia, short stature, hypotrichosis, variable degree of immune dysfunction and increased incidence of anaemia, Hirschsprung disease and malignancy."

PMID:22420014 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"If both parents are known to be heterozygous for an RMRP pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier."

Discussions and Knowledge Gaps

By what route does deficiency of a ubiquitously expressed non-coding RNA produce failure of enteric neural crest colonization, and why does this manifest as Hirschsprung disease in only a minority of patients?
KNOWLEDGE GAP OPEN gap_chh_hirschsprung_mechanism
Attached to
pathophysiology#Enteric Aganglionosis pathophysiology#Delayed G2-to-M Progression
The association between CHH and Hirschsprung disease is established, but the link from RMRP dysfunction to enteric aganglionosis is unknown. Reduced proliferation or migration of enteric neural crest cells is a testable hypothesis. Existing cell-cycle findings in other cell types do not establish that mechanism or explain incomplete penetrance. Hypoplastic gut in a model must also be distinguished from loss of enteric ganglia.
Proposed experiments
Enteric neural crest colonization under graded RMRP deficiency
exp_chh_enteric_crest_colonization
Track enteric neural crest cell proliferation, migration velocity and terminal colonization of the distal gut across a graded allelic series of RMRP deficiency, using the zebrafish model and patient-derived enteric neural crest-like cells, and test whether the colonization front fails to reach the hindgut within the developmental window. Measure Cyclin B2 turnover in the migrating population to test the cell-cycle account specifically.
Decision criterion
A dose-dependent colonization defect accompanied by impaired neural crest proliferation and rescue after RMRP correction would support this mechanism. Normal colonization in one model would limit its applicability but would not exclude effects of other alleles, developmental stages or species.
Supporting outcome
  • RMRP-dependent proliferation or migration defects contribute to impaired enteric neural crest colonization.
Refuting outcome
  • Colonization remains normal under the tested conditions despite documented RMRP dysfunction, weakening this model-specific hypothesis.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:42170584 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Hirschsprung's disease (HD) is a well-known comorbidity of CHH, although the pathogenetic link between RMRP deficiency and HD remains unknown."
Explicit statement in the review literature that this mechanism is unknown, which is what makes it a knowledge gap rather than an omission.
What are the relative contributions of immune dysfunction and cell-intrinsic RMRP effects to lymphoma susceptibility in CHH?
KNOWLEDGE GAP OPEN gap_chh_cancer_surveillance_versus_cell_autonomous
Attached to
pathophysiology#Malignancy Predisposition pathophysiology#Impaired Telomere Maintenance pathophysiology#Delayed G2-to-M Progression
Lymphoma risk is elevated, but its causal basis is unresolved. Malignancy can occur without preceding clinical immune symptoms; this does not demonstrate normal immune function or exclude impaired surveillance. Cell-cycle and telomere abnormalities measured in selected patient cells motivate investigation of intrinsic susceptibility, but have not been established in every tissue or in the malignant clone. Immune and intrinsic mechanisms may coexist, and cancer risk after HSCT is not determined by these observations.
Proposed experiments
Genomic and clonal characterization of CHH-associated lymphomas
exp_chh_lymphoma_clonal_origin
Sequence CHH-associated lymphomas for mutational signatures of replication stress and telomere crisis, quantify telomere length and cyclin dysregulation within the malignant clone against the patient's own non-malignant lymphocytes, and determine Epstein-Barr virus status systematically rather than opportunistically. Compare against sporadic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and against lymphomas arising in non-CHH immunodeficiencies.
Decision criterion
Enrichment of replication-stress or telomere-crisis signatures relative to appropriate lymphoma controls would support an intrinsic contribution, especially with functional validation. Absence of enrichment would be inconclusive about immune surveillance and other intrinsic mechanisms.
Supporting outcome
  • CHH-associated lymphomas show functionally supported intrinsic RMRP-related susceptibility in addition to any immune contribution.
Refuting outcome
  • The tested genomic signatures are not enriched, weakening those specific intrinsic hypotheses without proving a purely immune mechanism.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:10064668 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"This study confirms an increased risk of cancer, especially non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, probably attributable to defective immunity, among patients with CHH."
The surveillance attribution is offered as probable, not demonstrated, which is the opening this gap addresses.
PMID:31379817 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Of the 15 patients with non-skin cancer, eight had no preceding clinical symptoms of immunodeficiency."
Absence of prior clinical symptoms limits clinical prediction; it does not establish normal immune function.
How does loss of RMRP reduce telomerase activity when telomerase gene transcript levels are normal?
KNOWLEDGE GAP OPEN gap_chh_telomerase_post_transcriptional_mechanism
Attached to
pathophysiology#Impaired Telomere Maintenance
Reduced telomerase activity was not explained by relative telomerase-gene transcript levels in the studied lymphocytes. Protein abundance, assembly, localization and cell-state effects remain candidates. The reported TERT-RMRP complex has RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity and should not be equated with the telomerase holoenzyme. A relationship between impaired ribosome production and telomerase function is plausible but has not been demonstrated in CHH.
Proposed experiments
Localizing the post-transcriptional telomerase defect in CHH lymphocytes
exp_chh_telomerase_assembly_step
In patient lymphocytes across an allelic series, quantify TERT protein abundance, TERC levels, telomerase holoenzyme assembly and trafficking, and TERT-RMRP complex formation, and test whether restoring TERT protein alone rescues telomerase activity. Run the same panel in cells where ribosome synthesis is limited independently of RMRP, to separate a specific TERT-RMRP effect from a general translational ceiling.
Decision criterion
Identify which protein, assembly or trafficking defect tracks reduced activity and responds to RMRP correction. Reproduction by an independent ribosome perturbation would support a shared route, but specificity and mediation would require rescue experiments and control of cell activation and proliferation.
Supporting outcome
  • A specific post-transcriptional RMRP-telomerase mechanism independent of general ribosome limitation
Refuting outcome
  • Independent ribosome perturbation reproduces the defect, weakening a uniquely RMRP-specific explanation while leaving the mediating steps unresolved.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:28126377 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Telomerase deficiency in patients with CHH is not mediated by abnormal telomerase gene transcript levels relative to those of endogenous genes."
The measured relative transcript levels do not explain the activity deficit; the result does not establish one particular post-transcriptional mechanism.
PMID:28126377 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"These findings suggest that telomere deficiency is implicated in the CHH disease phenotype through an as yet unidentified mechanism."
The authors state directly that the mechanism is unidentified.
Does haematopoietic stem cell transplantation ever rescue linear growth in CHH, and if so, what distinguishes the patients in whom it does?
KNOWLEDGE GAP OPEN gap_chh_hsct_effect_on_linear_growth
Attached to
pathophysiology#Growth Plate Chondrocyte Differentiation Failure pathophysiology#Multilineage Bone Marrow Progenitor Failure
Reports of growth after HSCT differ: older summaries describe persistent growth failure, whereas GeneReviews reports catch-up growth, possibly related to fewer infections, and two promoter-variant cases reportedly normalized growth. Improved linear growth does not by itself establish reversal of skeletal dysplasia. Genotype, age, chronic illness, nutrition and conditioning may contribute to differences. These observations do not establish skeletal growth as an indication for HSCT.
Proposed experiments
Genotype-stratified growth trajectories before and after transplantation
exp_chh_growth_trajectory_after_hsct
Compare longitudinal height trajectories against CHH-specific curves before and after HSCT, with age- and genotype-matched untransplanted comparators. Record nutrition, infection burden, conditioning, pubertal development and skeletal imaging. Analyze promoter and transcribed-region variants separately where numbers permit, while accounting for indication and survivor bias.
Decision criterion
A reproducible change in growth trajectory would support an association with HSCT, while accompanying clinical and skeletal findings could distinguish catch-up growth from structural change. Observational comparisons alone would not establish causality or justify transplantation for growth.
Supporting outcome
  • A subgroup shows reproducible improvement in linear growth associated with HSCT after adjustment for major measured confounders.
Refuting outcome
  • No meaningful trajectory difference is detected within the precision and follow-up of the study.

Can conclusions about CHH pathogenesis be validated in a mammalian whole-organism system, given that Rmrp knockout mice die before embryonic day 6.5 while heterozygotes are healthy?
HUMAN MODEL MISMATCH OPEN mismatch_chh_no_viable_mouse_model
Attached to
pathophysiology#RMRP Non-Coding RNA Loss of Function pathophysiology#Growth Plate Chondrocyte Differentiation Failure
The reported mouse disruption is lethal before embryonic day 6.5, whereas heterozygotes are healthy despite reduced RMRP expression. This limits that model for studying the viable human disease, but does not exclude future hypomorphic or conditional models. Zebrafish knockouts permit developmental analysis before larval death and show partial pharmacological rescue; whether the same response occurs in a mammalian growth plate is unresolved. Mammalian cell and tissue studies provide complementary evidence without reproducing the complete organismal phenotype.
Proposed experiments
Hypomorphic and conditional Rmrp mouse alleles reproducing patient variants
exp_chh_hypomorphic_mouse_knockin
Generate knock-in mice carrying the founder n.71A>G variant and a promoter-region insertion allele, plus a chondrocyte-conditional deletion, and characterize growth-plate architecture, limb proportion, immune reconstitution and erythropoiesis. Test whether beta-catenin inhibition rescues the skeletal phenotype in a mammalian growth plate as it partially does in zebrafish.
Decision criterion
A viable hypomorphic or tissue-specific allele that reproduces relevant patient phenotypes would enable mammalian tests of the proposed pathway. Failure of the selected constructs would limit those designs, not prove that no murine disease model can exist.
Supporting outcome
  • A graded mammalian model of RMRP deficiency is achievable and can validate the zebrafish rescue
Refuting outcome
  • The tested alleles fail to reproduce the relevant phenotype, requiring alternative dosage, tissue or developmental designs.

Pathophysiology

24
RMRP Promoter Expansion
Insertions, duplications, and triplications between the RMRP TATA box and transcription start site can impair promoter function. These are regulatory alleles of a noncoding RNA gene. CHH requires an affected second allele; a promoter allele may be paired with a transcribed-region allele, and surviving patients with biallelic promoter variants have been reported.

Reduced RMRP Transcript Abundance Promoter spacing alterations impair transcription in functional assays; reduced transcript abundance was also observed in a homozygous promoter-duplication patient.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:11207361 SUPPORT In Vitro
"Insertion mutations immediately upstream of the coding sequence silence transcription while mutations in the transcribed region do not."
The original functional study distinguished upstream insertion effects on transcription from the tested transcribed-region variants. Its reference to coding sequence means the transcribed noncoding RNA, not a protein-coding region.
PMID:37115363 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"This study provides further evidence that homozygous RMRP promoter duplications reduce but do not abrogate transcript expression and are not universally embryonically lethal."
The homozygous promoter-duplication case refutes universal embryonic lethality of this allele class.
Reduced RMRP Transcript Abundance
Reduced availability of the RMRP RNA is one route to functional deficiency, particularly for promoter expansion alleles. The measured reduction in a promoter-duplication patient does not distinguish expression changes across all tissues from cell-type-specific effects. Transcribed-region variants need not reduce total RNA abundance.

RMRP Non-Coding RNA Loss of Function Reduced availability of the RNA component limits RMRP-dependent activity. The amount of residual RNA and the consequences in individual tissues depend on the alleles.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:37115363 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"The patient was found to have severely reduced RMRP transcript abundance (P < 0.01)"
Transcript quantification in a patient with a homozygous promoter duplication supports reduced RNA abundance. A single blood-derived measurement does not establish the expression pattern in every tissue.
RMRP Transcribed-Region Variants
Pathogenic substitutions and small sequence alterations affect the transcribed noncoding RNA. They may alter RNA structure or interactions rather than change a protein sequence. The founder variant is n.71A>G on NR_003051.3, termed 70AG in older functional literature. The consequences of this experimentally studied allele should not be assigned to all transcribed-region variants.

Reduced Intact RNase MRP Complex
Engineered K562 cells homozygous for the founder substitution have less intact RNase MRP complex and reduced RNA association of POP1 and RPP38. Total RMRP abundance is preserved, and SHAPE probing shows subtle local flexibility changes rather than extensive RNA refolding. Impaired complex stability is supported for this allele and cell system; the exact structural mechanism remains unresolved.

PMID:35115551 SUPPORT INDIRECT In Vitro

RMRP Non-Coding RNA Loss of Function
RMRP encodes the untranslated RNA component of RNase MRP. Disease-associated alleles reduce RNA availability or impair RNA-dependent function by allele-specific mechanisms. Promoter effects and impaired complex stability are distinct routes. Complete RMRP deficiency is lethal in experimental models, but these observations do not establish that every human disease allele retains activity or that all biallelic promoter variants are lethal.

Downstream
Impaired Pre-rRNA Processing RMRP dysfunction delays pre-rRNA processing in engineered cells and patient-derived fibroblasts.
Delayed G2-to-M Progression Founder-variant patient fibroblasts show delayed mitotic entry. The experiments did not isolate a single causal transcript or demonstrate rescue by restoring RMRP.
Impaired Telomere Maintenance Patient lymphocytes exhibit impaired telomere homeostasis, but the mechanism linking RMRP variants to telomerase deficiency is unresolved. The TERT-RMRP complex has RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity and is not the telomerase holoenzyme.
Reduced RMRP-Derived Small RNA Abundance Patient-derived cell lines have reduced RMRP-derived small RNAs; how different alleles affect their production or stability remains uncertain.
Intestinal Enteropathy Gastrointestinal manifestations are associated with biallelic RMRP disease; the intervening mechanisms have not been demonstrated.
Impaired RNase MRP-Dependent mRNA Turnover Reduced Rmrp activity alters the abundance of mRNA substrates in experimental cells; the effects depend on allele and cellular context.
Reduced Thymic T-Cell Output CHH is associated with reduced thymic output; the intervening molecular steps are incompletely defined.
Increased Activation-Induced T-Cell Death Patient RMRP genotypes are associated with increased activation-induced lymphocyte death; the responsible molecular mediator is unresolved.
Malignancy Predisposition Biallelic RMRP disease is associated with increased cancer risk, through unresolved immune and cell-intrinsic pathways.
Enteric Aganglionosis Hirschsprung disease is associated with CHH, with no established sequence of molecular intermediates.
Multilineage Bone Marrow Progenitor Failure Functional marrow progenitor impairment is observed in CHH; its molecular intermediates and relationship to peripheral blood counts remain unresolved.

Impaired Pre-rRNA Processing
RNase MRP dysfunction delays processing of pre-rRNA in ITS1. Patient-derived fibroblasts and engineered founder-variant K562 cells show altered precursor ratios consistent with reduced site-2 cleavage. In the engineered cells, the ratio of mature short to long 5.8S rRNA is unchanged; older qPCR findings of extended species may instead reflect accumulated precursors. The findings support a processing defect without requiring the same precursor profile in every cell type.

Reduced Cytosolic Ribosome Abundance
Founder-variant K562 cells have reduced per-cell mature rRNA and a reduced ratio of cytosolic to mitochondrial ribosomes. RNA-associated proteomics and total-proteome measurements support this finding. These are measurements of abundance and relative pools, not proof of a changed protein composition of each ribosome. High biosynthetic demand is a candidate explanation for tissue vulnerability rather than an established account of all CHH manifestations.

Impaired RNase MRP-Dependent mRNA Turnover
RNase MRP has reported mRNA-processing functions in addition to pre-rRNA processing. Rmrp knockdown increases cyclin B2 and viperin transcript abundance in ATDC5 cells. Functional studies across RMRP alleles associate impaired mRNA cleavage with extraskeletal features. The contribution of individual substrates to patient lymphocyte, marrow, and hair abnormalities remains unresolved; these findings do not identify cyclin B2 as the proven cause of the separately measured G2 delay in patient fibroblasts.

"Reduced Rmrp RNA levels indeed resulted in elevated levels of RNase MRP substrates Clb2 and Viperin mRNAs, as well as an accumulation of an ITS1 pre-rRNA processing intermediate."

Delayed G2-to-M Progression
Fibroblasts from five adults homozygous for the founder RMRP variant proliferate slowly and are delayed before mitotic entry. EdU labeling and time-lapse imaging localized the delay to G2; S-phase and mitotic duration were largely preserved, without excess cell death. Transcriptomics implicates multiple cell-cycle regulators. These observations do not establish impaired cyclin B2 RNA cleavage as the specific cause of the G2 delay.

Impaired Telomere Maintenance
Patient lymphocyte subsets show shortened telomeres and reduced telomerase activity. Normal relative transcript levels for telomerase components did not explain the activity defect. The mechanism remains unidentified. RMRP binding to TERT in some cell lines forms an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex and does not establish a direct role in the telomerase holoenzyme. A separate case-control study found shorter telomeres particularly in children, without an association between relative telomere length and clinical or laboratory features within CHH.

Reduced RMRP-Derived Small RNA Abundance
RMRP produces the short RNAs RMRP-S1 and RMRP-S2. Their steady-state levels were reduced in two founder-variant patient fibroblast lines and one patient-derived B-cell line. Production is Dicer-dependent in HEK293 cells, but the route from each disease allele to reduced small-RNA abundance is unresolved. Abundance changes in these cell lines do not establish loss of silencing activity in hair follicles or growth plates.

Growth Plate Chondrocyte Differentiation Failure
RMRP expression rises during hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation in mouse growth plates and ATDC5 cultures. Rmrp knockdown impairs hypertrophic markers, matrix accumulation, and mineralization in vitro. Patient fibroblasts induced toward a chondrocyte-like state also show reduced hypertrophic differentiation. These models support a role for RMRP in cartilage maturation, consistent with the paucity and disorganization of growth-plate chondrocytes in CHH. The responsible RNA substrates and relative contributions of ribosome synthesis, cell-cycle regulation, and small RNAs remain unresolved. Wnt/beta-catenin activation and partial pharmacological rescue are findings from the zebrafish model, not established human mechanisms.

Impaired T-Lymphocyte Proliferation
Peripheral T cells from patients with CHH can proliferate poorly after stimulation. Experiments demonstrate altered cell-cycle distribution and increased activation-induced death; Rmrp disruption in primary mouse T-cell cultures also impairs expansion and pre-rRNA processing. These findings support cell-intrinsic dysfunction, but the relative contributions of RNA processing, telomere homeostasis, and other pathways remain unresolved.

Reduced numbers of recent thymic emigrants indicate impaired thymic T-cell generation. This phenotype can occur even without clinically significant immunodeficiency and need not imply a uniform thymic architectural defect in all patients.

Increased Activation-Induced T-Cell Death
Activated patient lymphocyte cultures show increased apoptosis or late apoptotic/necrotic cell fractions. This contributes to reduced expansion alongside cell-cycle abnormalities. The result is specific to stimulated lymphocytes and should not be generalized to patient fibroblasts, where increased death was not detected.

Cellular and Humoral Immune Dysfunction
Immune dysfunction ranges from laboratory abnormalities without frequent infections to symptomatic humoral or combined immunodeficiency, including SCID in some patients. T-cell counts, naive subsets, and recent thymic emigrants can be reduced; B-cell and antibody defects are variable. Clinical progression, including adult-onset disease, occurs in a subset rather than universally. Clinical history, function testing, and serial assessment are needed together.

Multilineage Bone Marrow Progenitor Failure
A study of eight patients with a history of anemia found reduced erythroid, megakaryocyte, and usually granulocyte-macrophage colony formation. Stronger stimulation revealed normal or increased erythroid progenitor numbers, supporting functional impairment rather than simple depletion. The culture defect did not correlate with peripheral blood counts. Clinical anemia is often macrocytic and more severe in early childhood, but persistent transfusion dependence occurs in a severe subgroup.

Immune Dysregulation and Autoimmunity
Clinical autoimmune manifestations occurred in 11 of 104 Finnish patients and were associated with higher mortality and recurrent serious infections. Autoantibody positivity can occur without corresponding clinical disease. The mechanisms of impaired tolerance remain uncertain; normal regulatory T-cell counts do not exclude functional defects. Asthma and rhinitis diagnoses are common, but not all reported respiratory symptoms have demonstrated allergic mechanisms.

Malignancy Predisposition
CHH confers increased risk of lymphoma and basal cell carcinoma. Both defective immune surveillance and cell-intrinsic consequences of RMRP dysfunction are proposed contributors, but neither explains all cases. Malignancy can develop without preceding clinical immunodeficiency. Normal cancer incidence among unaffected relatives supports a disease association without ruling out environmental contributions, including the contribution of sun exposure to skin cancer risk.

Chronic Airway Injury
Recurrent infection and inflammation can contribute to structural lung disease in CHH. Bronchiectasis can occur without hypogammaglobulinemia and its course is variable. The follow-up MRI study found stable or improved imaging in 14 participants over a median 6.8 years, but two of the three participants with established bronchiectasis lacked repeat imaging. This selected cohort cannot establish the course of advanced bronchiectasis. Lung disease is an important cause of mortality, without having the highest cause-specific standardized mortality ratio in the longitudinal mortality study.
Downstream
Bronchiectasis Repeated airway infection and inflammation produce irreversible bronchial dilatation.
Recurrent pneumonia Impaired clearance and damaged airways predispose to repeated pneumonia.

Abnormal Hair Production
Mechanism confidence: Hypothetical
An incompletely resolved defect of hair production underlies the fine or sparse hair typical of CHH. Functional allele comparisons associate hair hypoplasia with reduced mRNA cleavage, and small-RNA perturbation studies identify a candidate regulatory route. Neither result establishes a unique molecular cause in patient follicles. Hair appearance is variable, including normal hair in some patients; direct follicular histology is not established by the cited clinical descriptions.
Downstream

Intestinal Enteropathy
Persistent or recurrent diarrhea in CHH may accompany malabsorption or enteropathy. In the Finnish cohort, duodenal villous atrophy occurred in some patients despite negative celiac testing. Infection and immune dysregulation are possible contributors; systematic histology was limited and a single mechanism has not been established. This process is distinct from congenital enteric aganglionosis.
Downstream
Chronic diarrhea Enteropathy is one potential cause of chronic diarrhea; infectious and other causes also require evaluation.

Enteric Aganglionosis
Hirschsprung disease occurs at increased frequency in CHH. The developmental link between RMRP dysfunction and absent enteric ganglion cells is unknown; intestinal epithelial abnormalities in zebrafish do not establish the cause of human aganglionosis.

Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
Action: hematopoietic cell transplantationNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is hematopoietic cell transplantation (NCIT:C15431). NCIT:C15431 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation NCIT:C15431
Platform: Cell therapy
Allogeneic HSCT can correct severe immune dysfunction and transfusion-dependent anemia. In a historical European series of 16 transplanted patients, 10 were long-term survivors, with normalization of T-cell numbers and function and resolution of autoimmunity. Skeletal dysplasia is not established as corrected by HSCT, although catch-up growth has been reported, possibly because infections decrease. Indications in mildly symptomatic patients remain debated; timing should account for severe infections, organ damage, and malignancy.
Mechanism Target:
RESTORES Impaired T-Lymphocyte Proliferation — Replacing the haematopoietic compartment with donor cells carrying functional RMRP restores lymphocyte numbers and function.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:20375313 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"T-lymphocyte numbers and function have normalized, and autoimmunity has resolved in all survivors."
Direct evidence that transplantation corrects the lymphoid arm modeled by this node.
RESTORES Multilineage Bone Marrow Progenitor Failure — Donor progenitors restore erythropoiesis, curing transfusion-dependent anemia.
Show evidence (1 reference)

RESTORES Immune Dysregulation and Autoimmunity — Autoimmunity resolved in all long-term survivors of transplantation, consistent with the dysregulation being intrinsic to the haematopoietic compartment.

Immunoglobulin replacement therapy
Action: immunoglobulin therapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is immunoglobulin therapy (NCIT:C62710). NCIT:C62710 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Immunoglobulin Therapy NCIT:C62710
Platform: Other
Immunoglobulin replacement is considered for clinically relevant antibody deficiency, including low immunoglobulin or IgG subclass levels or inadequate vaccine responses. It supplies passive antibody but does not correct the underlying cellular defect; lung disease can progress despite treatment.
Mechanism Target:
BYPASSES Cellular and Humoral Immune Dysfunction — Passive antibody supplements inadequate humoral immunity without correcting the underlying RMRP-related defect.

Live viral vaccination after specialist immune assessment
Action: vaccinationNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is vaccination (NCIT:C15346). NCIT:C15346 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Vaccination NCIT:C15346
Platform: Vaccine
Live vaccines require individualized specialist assessment and are avoided in severe or clinically significant combined immunodeficiency. The Finnish study supports consideration in selected patients with no or mild clinical immune dysfunction. All five prospective varicella vaccine recipients had normal mitogen responses and normal IgG, although three were lymphopenic. One developed self-limited rash and knee swelling. This small, selected trial does not establish safety across the CHH spectrum; mild lymphopenia alone was not an absolute exclusion in the study.

Severe anemia is managed with red cell transfusion, and iron chelation is recommended for those requiring repeated transfusion. Growth hormone therapy, generally not recommended
Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Platform: Peptide
Routine growth hormone treatment is not recommended because sustained benefit has not been established. A review describes eight patients with ineffective or temporary responses, but also reports improvement in a child without growth hormone deficiency. A later case report describes improved growth during approximately two years of treatment without final-height follow-up. Coexisting growth hormone deficiency warrants endocrine assessment, although replacement does not guarantee a growth response. These heterogeneous observations do not demonstrate correction of the underlying chondrocyte defect. Growth hormone did not improve erythroid colony formation in the cited anemia study.

Sirolimus for anemia, single-case evidence
Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Agent: Sirolimus NCIT:C1212 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses Sirolimus (NCIT:C1212). NCIT:C1212 is a therapeutic agent from the NCI Thesaurus.
One patient with a clinical CHH diagnosis and ALPS-like immune dysregulation had improved anemia and erythroid colony growth during sirolimus treatment, deterioration after withdrawal, and improvement after restarting. Immune deficiency nevertheless progressed and ultimately required HSCT after cryptococcal meningoencephalitis. Both RMRP variants remained formally uncertain without functional validation, and somatic FAS disease was not excluded. This report is exploratory evidence, not an established CHH treatment or demonstration of a specific mTOR-mediated rescue mechanism.

Diagnosis

6
Clinical and radiographic diagnosis
Diagnosis is established in a proband with characteristic clinical and radiographic findings. Metaphyseal changes may be absent in the first two years of life and some patients never show them, so normal radiographs do not exclude CHH.
skeletal radiography NCIT:C38101 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT)
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:22420014 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Diagnosis of a CHH-AD spectrum disorder is established in a proband with characteristic clinical and radiographic findings."
States the clinical and radiographic basis of diagnosis.
PMID:42170584 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Some patients' radiographs show no signs of metaphyseal dysplasia despite evident short stature (19) or severe immunodeficiency"
Supports the caveat that radiographic normality does not exclude the diagnosis.
Molecular genetic testing
Identification of biallelic RMRP variants confirms the diagnosis and enables family studies, carrier testing and prenatal or preimplantation testing. Testing must specifically cover the non-coding gene including its promoter region, since standard exome capture may miss it; whole-genome sequencing, targeted panels fully covering RMRP, or copy-number assessment are the reliable options.
molecular genetic testing NCIT:C19770 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT)
Show evidence (2 references)

Specifies the role of molecular testing relative to clinical diagnosis.
PMID:42170584 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"diagnostic approach can include whole-genome sequencing or targeted panels that fully capture the RMRP gene, including the promoter region, as well as copy number variation assessment"
Specifies the testing strategies that reliably cover a non-coding gene and its promoter.
Immunological assessment and surveillance
Baseline and serial assessment includes lymphocyte subsets and function, immunoglobulins, and age-appropriate vaccine responses. Immunophenotyping is one component of this broader evaluation. Laboratory abnormalities and clinical severity do not always align; progression can occur, including in adulthood, but is not universal.
Immunological Flow Cytometry NCIT:C113003 NCI Thesaurus (NCIT)
The ontology binding represents flow-cytometric immunophenotyping; proliferation, immunoglobulin and vaccine-response tests complement it.

Directly supports assessing asymptomatic patients rather than testing on symptoms alone.
PMID:31379817 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"In conclusion, patients with CHH may develop adult-onset immunodeficiency or malignancy without preceding clinical symptoms of immune defect, warranting careful follow-up."
The prospective-cohort conclusion that makes lifelong surveillance the recommended model rather than symptom-triggered testing.
PMID:28284971 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"SAD may therefore be a marker of more severe disease and vaccine responses should be routinely studied after infancy."
Supports routine vaccine-response testing as part of immunological assessment.
Malignancy surveillance
Regular malignancy surveillance includes clinical and laboratory assessment and appropriate imaging. GeneReviews specifies annual examination and abdominal ultrasound every one to two years in children, with adult evaluation according to clinical needs. Follow-up continues beyond childhood because malignancy can develop without preceding clinical immune symptoms. Cohort observations support early detection but do not quantify the independent benefit of a particular screening schedule.

Growth and musculoskeletal surveillance
Follow linear growth using CHH-specific curves and assess lower-limb joints and the spine clinically, with radiographs when indicated. The separate recommendation for routine annual spine radiography in anauxetic dysplasia should not be generalized to all patients with CHH.

Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:22420014 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Monitor growth using CHH-specific growth curves; clinical and (if warranted) radiographic examination of joints of the lower extremities and spine annually in childhood and as required in adulthood;"
Clinical monitoring and conditional radiography are recommended for the CHH spectrum.
Pregnancy and neonatal assessment
For an affected mother, GeneReviews advises considering planned cesarean delivery because of cephalopelvic disproportion. This differs from an unaffected mother carrying an affected fetus, for whom fetal CHH alone does not establish a cesarean indication. Prenatal short long bones can prompt genetic evaluation. Neonates require assessment for respiratory compromise, anemia, immune dysfunction and Hirschsprung disease; available neonatal frequencies come from a small retrospective Finnish cohort with incomplete records.

Differential Diagnoses

5

Conditions with similar clinical presentations that must be differentiated from Cartilage-hair hypoplasia:

Anauxetic dysplasia MONDO:0011773
Overlapping Features The severe end of the same RMRP spectrum, reached by allele combinations producing the greatest loss of rRNA cleavage activity. It shares the molecular lesion but is skeletally far more severe and may include atlantoaxial subluxation and cognitive deficiency, while the hair, immune and haematologic features characteristic of CHH are not assumed to be present.
Distinguishing Features
  • Markedly more severe skeletal dysplasia, with the most pronounced short stature of the spectrum.
  • Atlantoaxial subluxation may be present in the newborn, which is not characteristic of CHH.
  • Cognitive deficiency may occur, which is not a feature of CHH.
  • Hair, immune and haematologic involvement is conditional rather than characteristic.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:17701897 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Mutations in the RMRP gene lead to a wide spectrum of autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasias, ranging from the milder phenotypes metaphyseal dysplasia without hypotrichosis and cartilage hair hypoplasia (CHH) to the severe anauxetic dysplasia (AD)."
Places CHH and anauxetic dysplasia at different points of one allelic spectrum.
PMID:22420014 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"The most severe phenotype, AD, has the most pronounced skeletal phenotype, may be associated with atlantoaxial subluxation in the newborn, and may include cognitive deficiency."
Names the features that separate anauxetic dysplasia from CHH clinically.
Metaphyseal dysplasia without hypotrichosis Not Yet Curated MONDO:0009601
Overlapping Features The mild end of the same RMRP spectrum, distinguished from CHH by absence of hair involvement. Its status as a separate entity is doubtful: longitudinal follow-up of such individuals has revealed late-onset immune abnormalities typical of CHH, so the distinction may reflect age at assessment rather than a different disease.
Distinguishing Features
  • Absence of hypotrichosis, as reflected in the disease name.
  • Milder skeletal phenotype than CHH.
  • May be reclassified as CHH on longer follow-up once immune features emerge.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:17701897 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"Mutations in the RMRP gene lead to a wide spectrum of autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasias, ranging from the milder phenotypes metaphyseal dysplasia without hypotrichosis and cartilage hair hypoplasia (CHH) to the severe anauxetic dysplasia (AD)."
Places metaphyseal dysplasia without hypotrichosis at the mild end of the same spectrum as CHH.
PMID:42170584 SUPPORT Human Clinical
"However, the longitudinal follow-up of such individuals has revealed late-onset development of immune abnormalities typical for CHH."
Supports treating the distinction as provisional rather than a firm diagnostic boundary.
Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia MONDO:0007983
Overlapping Features Autosomal dominant COL10A1-related metaphyseal dysplasia shares short stature and radiographic metaphyseal abnormalities with CHH. The absence of the characteristic extraskeletal manifestations of CHH helps distinguish it.
Distinguishing Features
  • Autosomal dominant COL10A1-related disease rather than autosomal recessive RMRP-related disease.
  • Metaphyseal dysplasia, especially of the proximal femur, without the characteristic extraskeletal manifestations of CHH.
Show evidence (1 reference)
url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK84550/pdf/Bookshelf_NBK84550.pdf SUPPORT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"COL10A1 COL10A1-related metaphyseal dysplasia Schmid (See Schmid Metaphyseal Chondrodysplasia.) AD Short stature & radiographic metaphyseal abnormalities (metaphyseal dysplasia esp in proximal femur) resembling CHH No extraskeletal manifestations"
The GeneReviews differential table directly identifies the gene, inheritance, overlap and distinguishing features. Full-text PDF of the GeneReviews chapter, PMID:22420014.
Shwachman-Diamond syndrome MONDO:0009833
Overlapping Features Shwachman-Diamond syndrome overlaps with CHH through short stature, metaphyseal abnormalities, infections and anemia. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, neutropenia and poor weight gain are prominent distinguishing features; skeletal changes are usually milder.
Distinguishing Features
  • Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and poor weight gain are principal manifestations.
  • Neutropenia is a principal hematologic feature.
  • Skeletal features are usually milder than in CHH.
Show evidence (1 reference)
url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK84550/pdf/Bookshelf_NBK84550.pdf SUPPORT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"• Milder skeletal features (usually) • Principal manifestations: exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, neutropenia, poor weight gain, & growth deficiency"
The Shwachman-Diamond row in the GeneReviews differential table directly supports these distinctions. Full-text PDF of the GeneReviews chapter, PMID:22420014.
Dyskeratosis congenita MONDO:0015780
Overlapping Features Dyskeratosis congenita and related telomere biology disorders overlap with CHH through marrow failure, immune abnormalities, malignancy susceptibility and short telomeres. The classic mucocutaneous triad favors dyskeratosis congenita, whereas metaphyseal dysplasia and disproportionate short-limb stature favor CHH; neither diagnosis requires every characteristic finding.
Distinguishing Features
  • Classic mucocutaneous triad of dysplastic nails, reticular skin pigmentation and oral leukoplakia, which is not present in every patient.
  • Metaphyseal dysplasia and disproportionate short-limb stature favor CHH.
  • Caused by telomere maintenance genes rather than by RMRP.

Explicitly names the phenotypic overlap that makes this a mechanistically motivated differential.

"Classic DC is characterized by a triad of dysplastic nails, lacy reticular pigmentation of the upper chest and/or neck, and oral leukoplakia, although this may not be present in all individuals."

Animal Models

1
rmrp knockout zebrafish
Rmrp knockout zebrafish permit study of early chondrogenesis, ossification, cell proliferation and apoptosis, but survive only 12-14 days. Canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is increased, and pharmacological inhibition partly alleviates skeletal abnormalities. This is preclinical developmental evidence; efficacy in mammalian CHH or patients has not been established.

Growth Plate Chondrocyte Differentiation Failure partially recapitulates fidelity: moderate Reproduces dysregulated chondrogenesis and abnormal ossification, and implicates Wnt/beta-catenin as a reversible effector.
Limitations: Zebrafish cartilage development differs architecturally from the mammalian endochondral growth plate, and the primary readouts are pharyngeal arch patterning and skull and vertebral ossification rather than long-bone metaphyseal growth; ossification effects are directionally mixed, being inhibited in skull and promoted in vertebrae, which has no clean human counterpart.

Interpretation: Whole-organism correlate of the cartilage differentiation node; ALTERED rather than DECREASED because ossification changed in opposite directions in different skeletal elements.

name: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia
creation_date: "2026-08-14T00:00:00Z"
description: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is an autosomal recessive immuno-osseous dysplasia caused by biallelic variants in the noncoding RNA gene RMRP. Its variable manifestations include metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, disproportionate short stature, fine or sparse hair, immune dysfunction, anemia, Hirschsprung disease and increased malignancy risk. Promoter variants can reduce RNA expression, while transcribed-region variants can impair RNase MRP complex function. Studies demonstrate defective pre-rRNA processing, altered ribosome abundance and cell-proliferation defects; the contributions of mRNA turnover, small-RNA regulation and telomere homeostasis to individual tissues remain incompletely resolved. Immune dysfunction may become clinically apparent in adulthood, and malignancy can occur without preceding clinical immune symptoms.

inheritance:
- name: Autosomal recessive inheritance
  description: >-
    CHH is autosomal recessive, arising from biallelic variants in RMRP.
    Heterozygous carriers are asymptomatic and do not show the cellular
    proliferation defect, although telomerase activity is reduced in carriers in
    a gene-dose-dependent manner, so the carrier state is not entirely silent at
    every molecular level. Each sib of an affected individual has a 25%
    recurrence risk.
  inheritance_term:
    preferred_term: Autosomal recessive inheritance
    term:

    snippet: "Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is an autosomal recessive syndromic immunodeficiency with skeletal dysplasia, short stature, hypotrichosis, variable degree of immune dysfunction and increased incidence of anaemia, Hirschsprung disease and malignancy."
    explanation: >-
      States the autosomal recessive mode of inheritance alongside the defining
      multisystem phenotype.
  - reference: PMID:22420014
    reference_title: "Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia – Anauxetic Dysplasia Spectrum Disorders."
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: "If both parents are known to be heterozygous for an RMRP pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier."
    explanation: >-
      GeneReviews recurrence risks used in counselling families.

pathophysiology:
- name: RMRP Promoter Expansion
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Insertions, duplications, and triplications between the RMRP TATA box and transcription start site can impair promoter function. These are regulatory alleles of a noncoding RNA gene. CHH requires an affected second allele; a promoter allele may be paired with a transcribed-region allele, and surviving patients with biallelic promoter variants have been reported.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:11207361
    reference_title: Mutations in the RNA component of RNase MRP cause a pleiotropic human disease, cartilage-hair hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: Insertion mutations immediately upstream of the coding sequence silence transcription while mutations in the transcribed region do not.
    explanation: The original functional study distinguished upstream insertion effects on transcription from the tested transcribed-region variants. Its reference to coding sequence means the transcribed noncoding RNA, not a protein-coding region.
  - reference: PMID:37115363
    reference_title: Homozygous RMRP Promoter Duplications Cause Severely Reduced Transcript Abundance and SCID Associated with Cartilage Hair Hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: This study provides further evidence that homozygous RMRP promoter duplications reduce but do not abrogate transcript expression and are not universally embryonically lethal.
    explanation: The homozygous promoter-duplication case refutes universal embryonic lethality of this allele class.

      snippet: As shown in Fig 2, both the absolute and relative numbers of RTEs were significantly reduced in the patients with CHH, regardless of their age, compared with published normal values.
      explanation: Reduced recent thymic emigrants support decreased thymic output, including in patients without significant clinical infections.
  - target: Increased Activation-Induced T-Cell Death
    description: Patient RMRP genotypes are associated with increased activation-induced lymphocyte death; the responsible molecular mediator is unresolved.

      explanation: Annexin-V/7-AAD assays measured increased activation-associated cell death in patient lymphocyte cultures; significance depended on the assay condition.
  - target: Malignancy Predisposition
    description: Biallelic RMRP disease is associated with increased cancer risk, through unresolved immune and cell-intrinsic pathways.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES

      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: During the follow-up (2,365 person-years; mean 19.2 years), 14 cases of cancer were diagnosed in the CHH cohort (expected number 2.0; SIR 7.0, CI 3.8-12). Non-Hodgkin lymphoma was the most frequent cancer type (n = 9; SIR 90.2, CI 39.0-180)
      explanation: Registry-based quantification of the overall and lymphoma-specific excess risk against population expectation.

- name: Impaired Pre-rRNA Processing
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: RNase MRP dysfunction delays processing of pre-rRNA in ITS1. Patient-derived fibroblasts and engineered founder-variant K562 cells show altered precursor ratios consistent with reduced site-2 cleavage. In the engineered cells, the ratio of mature short to long 5.8S rRNA is unchanged; older qPCR findings of extended species may instead reflect accumulated precursors. The findings support a processing defect without requiring the same precursor profile in every cell type.

    snippet: Human cells engineered with the most common CHH mutation (70AG in RMRP) show specifically impaired pre-rRNA processing, resulting in reduced mature rRNA and a reduced ratio of cytosolic to mitochondrial ribosomes.
    explanation: Engineered founder-variant cells show impaired processing and a reduced cytosolic-to-mitochondrial ribosome ratio; this does not demonstrate altered composition of individual ribosomes.

- name: Reduced Cytosolic Ribosome Abundance
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Founder-variant K562 cells have reduced per-cell mature rRNA and a reduced ratio of cytosolic to mitochondrial ribosomes. RNA-associated proteomics and total-proteome measurements support this finding. These are measurements of abundance and relative pools, not proof of a changed protein composition of each ribosome. High biosynthetic demand is a candidate explanation for tissue vulnerability rather than an established account of all CHH manifestations.

  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: RNase MRP has reported mRNA-processing functions in addition to pre-rRNA processing. Rmrp knockdown increases cyclin B2 and viperin transcript abundance in ATDC5 cells. - name: Delayed G2-to-M Progression
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Fibroblasts from five adults homozygous for the founder RMRP variant proliferate slowly and are delayed before mitotic entry. EdU labeling and time-lapse imaging localized the delay to G2; S-phase and mitotic duration were largely preserved, without excess cell death. Transcriptomics implicates multiple cell-cycle regulators. These observations do not establish impaired cyclin B2 RNA cleavage as the specific cause of the G2 delay.

- name: Impaired Telomere Maintenance
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Patient lymphocyte subsets show shortened telomeres and reduced telomerase activity. Normal relative transcript levels for telomerase components did not explain the activity defect. The mechanism remains unidentified. RMRP binding to TERT in some cell lines forms an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex and does not establish a direct role in the telomerase holoenzyme. A separate case-control study found shorter telomeres particularly in children, without an association between relative telomere length and clinical or laboratory features within CHH.
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: telomere maintenance
    term:
      id: GO:0000723
      label: telomere maintenance
    modifier: DECREASED

    reference_title: Defects in lymphocyte telomere homeostasis contribute to cellular immune phenotype in patients with cartilage-hair hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Here we show that telomere length and telomerase activity are impaired in primary lymphocyte subsets from patients with CHH.
    explanation: Direct measurement of both telomere length and telomerase activity in patient lymphocytes.

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Telomerase deficiency in patients with CHH is not mediated by abnormal telomerase gene transcript levels relative to those of endogenous genes.
    explanation: The measured relative transcript levels did not explain the activity defect; the result does not identify its mechanism.

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Compared with age-matched and sex-matched healthy controls, median RTL was significantly shorter in patients with CHH (n=40 pairs, 1.05 vs 1.21, p=0.017), but not in mutation carriers (n=48 pairs, 1.16 vs 1.10, p=0.224).
    explanation: Independent quantification of telomere shortening in a larger patient cohort.

    reference_title: Decreased telomere length in children with cartilage-hair hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: In patients with CHH, RTL showed no correlation with genotype, clinical or laboratory characteristics.
    explanation: 'Retained negative result: the telomere arm is real at the population level but does not explain individual clinical variation.'

- name: Growth Plate Chondrocyte Differentiation Failure
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: RMRP expression rises during hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation in mouse growth plates and ATDC5 cultures. Rmrp knockdown impairs hypertrophic markers, matrix accumulation, and mineralization in vitro. Patient fibroblasts induced toward a chondrocyte-like state also show reduced hypertrophic differentiation. These models support a role for RMRP in cartilage maturation, consistent with the paucity and disorganization of growth-plate chondrocytes in CHH. The responsible RNA substrates and relative contributions of ribosome synthesis, cell-cycle regulation, and small RNAs remain unresolved. Wnt/beta-catenin activation and partial pharmacological rescue are findings from the zebrafish model, not established human mechanisms.

      label: chondrocyte

    explanation: Direct chondrocyte evidence coupling impaired pre-rRNA processing to deranged differentiation in the same experiment.

- name: Impaired T-Lymphocyte Proliferation
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Peripheral T cells from patients with CHH can proliferate poorly after stimulation. Experiments demonstrate altered cell-cycle distribution and increased activation-induced death; Rmrp disruption in primary mouse T-cell cultures also impairs expansion and pre-rRNA processing. These findings support cell-intrinsic dysfunction, but the relative contributions of RNA processing, telomere homeostasis, and other pathways remain unresolved.

- name: Increased Activation-Induced T-Cell Death
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Activated patient lymphocyte cultures show increased apoptosis or late apoptotic/necrotic cell fractions. This contributes to reduced expansion alongside cell-cycle abnormalities. The result is specific to stimulated lymphocytes and should not be generalized to patient fibroblasts, where increased death was not detected.

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: As shown in Fig 6, the percentage of both early and late apoptotic cells was increased in patients with CHH versus healthy controls, reaching a statistically significant difference for late apoptotic/necrotic cells on culture with anti-CD3 mAb 1 IL-2
    explanation: Annexin-V/7-AAD assays measured increased activation-associated cell death in patient lymphocyte cultures; significance depended on the assay condition.

- name: Cellular and Humoral Immune Dysfunction
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: Immune dysfunction ranges from laboratory abnormalities without frequent infections to symptomatic humoral or combined immunodeficiency, including SCID in some patients. T-cell counts, naive subsets, and recent thymic emigrants can be reduced; B-cell and antibody defects are variable. Clinical progression, including adult-onset disease, occurs in a subset rather than universally. Clinical history, function testing, and serial assessment are needed together.

- name: Multilineage Bone Marrow Progenitor Failure
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: A study of eight patients with a history of anemia found reduced erythroid, megakaryocyte, and usually granulocyte-macrophage colony formation. Stronger stimulation revealed normal or increased erythroid progenitor numbers, supporting functional impairment rather than simple depletion. The culture defect did not correlate with peripheral blood counts. Clinical anemia is often macrocytic and more severe in early childhood, but persistent transfusion dependence occurs in a severe subgroup.

    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: The present study shows defective in vitro colony formation in all myeloid lineages in patients with CHH, which is in accordance with the suggestion of a common cell proliferation defect in CHH.
    explanation: Establishes that the marrow defect spans lineages and is read by the authors as the same proliferation defect seen elsewhere.
  - reference: PMID:7895753
    reference_title: Defective in-vitro colony formation of haematopoietic progenitors in patients with cartilage-hair hypoplasia and history of anaemia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: The impaired growth was not caused by a decreased number of progenitors as shown by erythroid cultures. The erythroid progenitors were incapable of colony formation in culture conditions sufficient for colony formation by normal progenitors.
    explanation: Distinguishes a functional proliferation defect from progenitor depletion, which is the specific claim this node makes.

- name: Immune Dysregulation and Autoimmunity
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: Clinical autoimmune manifestations occurred in 11 of 104 Finnish patients and were associated with higher mortality and recurrent serious infections. Autoantibody positivity can occur without corresponding clinical disease. The mechanisms of impaired tolerance remain uncertain; normal regulatory T-cell counts do not exclude functional defects. Asthma and rhinitis diagnoses are common, but not all reported respiratory symptoms have demonstrated allergic mechanisms.

    supports: SUPPORT

    snippet: Clinical autoimmunity was common (11/104, 10.6%) and included conditions previously undescribed in subjects with CHH (narcolepsy, psoriasis, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, and multifocal motor axonal neuropathy).
    explanation: Quantifies clinical autoimmunity and establishes the breadth of the spectrum.

- name: Malignancy Predisposition
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: CHH confers increased risk of lymphoma and basal cell carcinoma. Both defective immune surveillance and cell-intrinsic consequences of RMRP dysfunction are proposed contributors, but neither explains all cases. Malignancy can develop without preceding clinical immunodeficiency. Normal cancer incidence among unaffected relatives supports a disease association without ruling out environmental contributions, including the contribution of sun exposure to skin cancer risk.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:18698627
    reference_title: Extended follow-up of the Finnish cartilage-hair hypoplasia cohort confirms high incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and basal cell carcinoma.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: During the follow-up (2,365 person-years; mean 19.2 years), 14 cases of cancer were diagnosed in the CHH cohort (expected number 2.0; SIR 7.0, CI 3.8-12). Non-Hodgkin lymphoma was the most frequent cancer type (n = 9; SIR 90.2, CI 39.0-180)
    explanation: Registry-based quantification of the overall and lymphoma-specific excess risk against population expectation.
  - reference: PMID:18698627
    reference_title: Extended follow-up of the Finnish cartilage-hair hypoplasia cohort confirms high incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and basal cell carcinoma.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: In addition, ten patients had basal cell carcinoma of the skin (expected number 0.3; SIR 33.2, CI 16-61).
    explanation: Quantifies the second component of the cancer excess.
  - reference: PMID:10064668
    reference_title: Increased incidence of cancer in patients with cartilage-hair hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The cancer incidence among the siblings or the parents did not differ from the average cancer incidence in the Finnish population.
    explanation: No excess was detected in unaffected relatives; this comparison does not exclude environmental effects or gene-environment interactions in affected patients.
  - reference: PMID:10064668

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: This study confirms an increased risk of cancer, especially non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, probably attributable to defective immunity, among patients with CHH.
    explanation: The attribution to defective immunity is explicitly probable rather than experimentally established.

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The most common lymphoma type was diffuse large cell B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (6/16, 38%). Eight patients received chemotherapy (8/16, 50%), and two of them survived.
    explanation: Characterizes the dominant lymphoma subtype and the poor treatment outcome.

- name: Chronic Airway Injury
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: Recurrent infection and inflammation can contribute to structural lung disease in CHH. Bronchiectasis can occur without hypogammaglobulinemia and its course is variable. The follow-up MRI study found stable or improved imaging in 14 participants over a median 6.8 years, but two of the three participants with established bronchiectasis lacked repeat imaging. This selected cohort cannot establish the course of advanced bronchiectasis. Lung disease is an important cause of mortality, without having the highest cause-specific standardized mortality ratio in the longitudinal mortality study.

  - reference: PMID:33675005

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Patients with cartilage-hair hypoplasia are prone to recurrent respiratory tract infections, and the prevalence of bronchiectasis ranges from 29 to 52%.
    explanation: Reports bronchiectasis prevalence across differently selected cohorts; this sentence alone does not prove the direction of causality between infections and airway damage.

    supports: SUPPORT

    snippet: Altogether 20 patients had deceased (SMR = 7.0, 95%CI = 4.3-11); most commonly from malignancy (n = 7, SMR = 10, 95%CI = 4.1-21) and lung disease (n = 4, SMR = 46, 95%CI = 9.5-130).
    explanation: Quantifies overall and lung-disease mortality; the full paper reports a higher standardized mortality ratio for lymphoid neoplasms.

    reference_title: 'Pulmonary Follow-Up Imaging in Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia: a Prospective Cohort Study.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: In conclusion, our results suggest slow if any development of bronchiectasis in selected subjects with cartilage-hair hypoplasia.
    explanation: The follow-up evidence is from a selected cohort with limited repeat imaging in participants with established bronchiectasis.

    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT

    explanation: Establishes the dissociation between measurable antibody deficiency and lung disease, and the limits of replacement therapy.

- name: Abnormal Hair Production
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: An incompletely resolved defect of hair production underlies the fine or sparse hair typical of CHH. Functional allele comparisons associate hair hypoplasia with reduced mRNA cleavage, and small-RNA perturbation studies identify a candidate regulatory route. Neither result establishes a unique molecular cause in patient follicles. Hair appearance is variable, including normal hair in some patients; direct follicular histology is not established by the cited clinical descriptions.

    explanation: Establishes fine silky hair as a characteristic feature of the spectrum.

    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES

- name: Intestinal Enteropathy
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: Persistent or recurrent diarrhea in CHH may accompany malabsorption or enteropathy. In the Finnish cohort, duodenal villous atrophy occurred in some patients despite negative celiac testing. Infection and immune dysregulation are possible contributors; systematic histology was limited and a single mechanism has not been established. This process is distinct from congenital enteric aganglionosis.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:30410491
    reference_title: A Wide Spectrum of Autoimmune Manifestations and Other Symptoms Suggesting Immune Dysregulation in Patients With Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The presence of DVA in three subjects with negative celiac screen underscores the necessity for systematic endoscopic evaluation of CHH individuals with gastrointestinal complaints.
    explanation: A small number of patients had duodenal villous atrophy without positive celiac testing; this does not establish autoimmune enteropathy in all patients with diarrhea.
  downstream:
  - target: Chronic diarrhea
    description: Enteropathy is one potential cause of chronic diarrhea; infectious and other causes also require evaluation.
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:30410491
      reference_title: A Wide Spectrum of Autoimmune Manifestations and Other Symptoms Suggesting Immune Dysregulation in Patients With Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: The presence of DVA in three subjects with negative celiac screen underscores the necessity for systematic endoscopic evaluation of CHH individuals with gastrointestinal complaints.
      explanation: A small number of patients had duodenal villous atrophy without positive celiac testing; this does not establish autoimmune enteropathy in all patients with diarrhea.
- name: Enteric Aganglionosis
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: Hirschsprung disease occurs at increased frequency in CHH. The developmental link between RMRP dysfunction and absent enteric ganglion cells is unknown; intestinal epithelial abnormalities in zebrafish do not establish the cause of human aganglionosis.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Hirschsprung’s disease (HD) is a well-known comorbidity of CHH, although the pathogenetic link between RMRP deficiency and HD remains unknown.
    explanation: The association is established, while the mechanistic link is unresolved.
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
  downstream:
  - target: Aganglionic megacolon
    description: Absence of enteric ganglion cells produces the Hirschsprung phenotype.
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
phenotypes:
- name: Disproportionate short-limb short stature
  category: Growth
  description: Disproportionate short stature with short extremities, largely established before birth and progressive during infancy and puberty. Median adult height is 131 cm for men and 123 cm for women. Individuals of normal height with genetically confirmed CHH have been reported, so short stature is characteristic but not obligatory.
  frequency: VERY_FREQUENT
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Disproportionate short-limb short stature
    term:
      id: HP:0008873
      label: Disproportionate short-limb short stature
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:22420014
    reference_title: Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia – Anauxetic Dysplasia Spectrum Disorders.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: CHH-AD spectrum disorders are characterized by severe disproportionate (short-limb) short stature that is usually recognized in the newborn, and occasionally prenatally because of the short extremities.
    explanation: Establishes short-limb disproportionate short stature as a defining and near-universal feature of the spectrum, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The growth failure is progressive, particularly during the first year of life and during puberty, resulting in the median adult height of 131 cm for males and 123 cm for females
    explanation: Quantifies the adult height outcome described here.
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: While short stature was first thought to be invariably present in CHH patients, individuals with normal height have since been reported
    explanation: 'Retained qualification: short stature is characteristic but not obligatory, which is why the band is VERY_FREQUENT rather than obligate.'
  - reference: PMID:42063088
    reference_title: Perinatal outcomes in 35 children with cartilage hair hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: In the whole cohort 27/32 (84%) had a Z-score below −2.0.
    explanation: Birth length was often short in the Finnish neonatal cohort, but normal birth length did not exclude CHH.
- name: Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia
  category: Skeletal
  description: Metaphyseal dysplasia with flaring, cupping, widening, cysts, fragmentation and scalloping of the metaphyses, most marked at the knee. Changes may not be apparent in the first two years of life and some patients never show them, so normal radiographs do not exclude the diagnosis.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia
    term:
      id: HP:0005871
      label: Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Radiologically, metaphyseal abnormalities included flaring, cupping, widening, cysts, fragmentation, and scalloping of metaphyses in the tubular bones, particularly at the knee.
    explanation: Describes the specific radiographic metaphyseal changes of CHH.
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Importantly, metaphyseal changes may not be apparent in the first 2 years of life
    explanation: Supports the diagnostic caveat that early radiographs may be uninformative.
- name: Joint hypermobility
  category: Musculoskeletal
  description: Generalized ligamentous laxity, present in the large majority of patients and coexisting paradoxically with restricted elbow extension.
  frequency: VERY_FREQUENT
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Joint hypermobility
    term:
      id: HP:0001382

  evidence:

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: incomplete extension of elbows (present in 92%, 79/86 patients) despite overall ligamentous laxity (95%, 81/85)
    explanation: Reports ligamentous laxity in 95% (81/85), which maps to the VERY_FREQUENT band (80-100%).
- name: Limited elbow extension
  category: Musculoskeletal

  frequency: VERY_FREQUENT

- name: Genu varum
  category: Skeletal

- name: Short metacarpal
  category: Skeletal
  description: Marked shortening of the metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges with metaphyseal cupping and cone-shaped epiphyses, giving the characteristically short, pudgy hands with striking laxity of the small joints. No frequency band is assigned because the orthopaedic series describes the finding qualitatively rather than counting it.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Short metacarpal
    term:
      id: HP:0010049

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: There is marked shortening of the metacarpals, metatarsals, and phalanges, with metaphyseal cupping
    explanation: Directly describes the shortened metacarpals this phenotype records, in the largest reported orthopaedic series of CHH patients.
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Typical features in addition to short limbs include short hands

- name: Coxa vara
  category: Skeletal
  description: Reduced femoral neck-shaft angle on radiography, present in about a quarter of patients whose films were reviewed. Occasionally severe enough to warrant corrective osteotomy alongside the more common varus knee.

    snippet: In our series, 27 % of the cases where radiographs were reviewed (19/71) showed coxa vara radiographically.
    explanation: Reports coxa vara in 27% (19/71), which maps to the OCCASIONAL band (5-29%).
- name: Decreased specific antibody response to vaccination
  category: Immunologic
  description: Specific antibody deficiency can occur despite normal total immunoglobulin levels. Seven of eight selected patients tested after pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccination had deficient responses. This small tested subgroup supports functional assessment but does not establish a population-wide frequency or a validated prognostic marker.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Decreased specific antibody response to vaccination
    term:
      id: HP:0032140
      label: Decreased specific antibody response to vaccination
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28284971
    reference_title: Analysis of clinical and immunologic phenotype in a large cohort of children and adults with cartilage-hair hypoplasia.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Seven out of eight (88%) patients who agreed to receive Pneumovax® vaccine demonstrated specific antibody deficiency (SAD)
    explanation: 'Reports the vaccine-challenge result: seven of eight participants demonstrated specific antibody deficiency. No frequency band is assigned because only eight patients consented, so the proportion is not a population estimate.'
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: While B cell counts are often decreased, hypogammaglobulinemia is rare in patients with CHH; moreover, some individuals have hypergammaglobulinemia
    explanation: Establishes that total immunoglobulin concentration is usually preserved in CHH, which is why the humoral defect is curated here as an impaired specific antibody response rather than as decreased circulating immunoglobulin.
- name: Decreased total neutrophil count
  category: Hematologic
  description: Neutropenia occurs in single patients and may be intrinsic to the marrow defect or autoimmune in origin. It is reported alongside the anemia rather than instead of it, consistent with the multilineage colony-formation defect, but it is not a characteristic feature and no frequency band is assigned.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Decreased total neutrophil count
    term:
      id: HP:0001875
      label: Decreased total neutrophil count
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42170584
    reference_title: 'Cartilage-hair hypoplasia: A comprehensive review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Single patients also have neutropenia, either intrinsic or autoimmune
    explanation: Establishes neutropenia as an occasional feature and names both candidate mechanisms; the single-patient framing is why no frequency is assigned.
  - reference: PMID:25764362
    reference_title: 'Cartilage hair hypoplasia: characteristics and orthopaedic manifestations.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: CHH is associated with a broad spectrum of mild-to-moderate, cell-mediated immunodysfunction, including occasionally severe combined immune deficiency, neutropenia, lymphopenia, disordered erythrogenesis, and a predisposition to lymphoma
    explanation: Independent listing of neutropenia among the recognized haematologic features of CHH.
- name: Fine hair
  category: Dermatologic
  description: Fine, silky hair, one of the two features that name the disease.
  phenotype_term:

    reference_title: Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia – Anauxetic Dysplasia Spectrum Disorders.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Other findings include joint hypermobility, fine, silky hair, immunodeficiency, anemia, increased risk for malignancy, gastrointestinal dysfunction, and impaired spermatogenesis.
    explanation: Establishes fine silky hair as a characteristic feature.
- name: Sparse hair
  category: Dermatologic
  description: Hypoplastic, sparse scalp and body hair, ranging in severity up to complete alopecia in the most severely affected individuals.
